planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart and trellis the vigorous thorny canes. Fruiting occurs on second-year canes, typically late May through June in zones 7-9.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and provide a two-wire trellis to support the vigorous, thorny canes. Cheyenne is an erect University of Arkansas blackberry released in 1977, prized for its early-to-midseason ripening and consistently high yields, making it a longtime favorite for pick-your-own plantings. Berries are large, sweet, and firm with a distinctive hint of raspberry flavor, ripening ahead of most other Arkansas-bred thorny cultivars. Because it retains thorns, plant it where hand-harvesting around the canes is acceptable in exchange for its productivity and fruit quality. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 per plant to maintain vigor and berry size in subsequent years.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Fruit Breeding — Blackberry Cultivar History
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blackberry Variety Trials

common_name: Comanche Blackberry (Vigorous Erect Thorny Processing Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart and trellis the strong, moderately thorny canes. Fruiting occurs on second-year canes, typically late May through June in zones 6-9.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and trellis the strong, moderately thorny canes for easier harvest. Comanche is an erect University of Arkansas blackberry originating from a 1965 cross of Darrow and Brazos, a sister seedling of Cherokee, and long valued for consistently outyielding older varieties like Brazos. Berries are firm and well-flavored, and the vigorous, upright canes hold up well to mechanical harvesting, making Comanche a reliable choice for both processing plantings and home gardens across the Gulf South. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 canes per plant to sustain yield and cane vigor in following years.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Fruit Breeding — Blackberry Cultivar History
ISHS — The Blackberry Breeding Program at the University of Arkansas: Thirty-Plus Years of Progress
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blackberry Variety Trials

common_name: Aliceblue Rabbiteye Blueberry (Early-Season Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Aliceblue has a low chill requirement and is among the earliest-flowering and earliest-ripening rabbiteye cultivars. Plant with a compatible early-season pollinator other than Beckyblue, since the two are cross-incompatible.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, in full sun with a compatible early-season pollinator nearby. Aliceblue was released in 1978 by the University of Florida IFAS to give North and Central Florida growers a rabbiteye that fruits reliably across both high- and low-chill winters, and it remains one of the earliest-flowering, earliest-ripening rabbiteye selections available. Berries are medium-sized and sweet on a vigorous, spreading bush. Because it flowers very early, site it with good air drainage to reduce frost risk to blooms during a late cold snap, and pair it with a pollinizer other than Beckyblue due to known cross-incompatibility between the two. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, mulch well, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain productive new fruiting canes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Blueberry Variety Profiles
